The story skillfully contrasts the working-class perspective of the narrator with the upper-class, image-conscious perspective of her mother-in-law, Miss Emily. Initially, Miss Emily is presented as a difficult, critical, and seemingly snobbish character who "audits" the narrator and calls her weekly to point out her flaws in grammar and posture. However, her perspective is rendered with great depth and believability. The narrator comes to realize that Miss Emily only criticizes things that can be changed—viewing this "editing" as a form of investment and respect. In the end, it is revealed that Miss Emily was also a grocery store cashier for eight years before building her real estate empire. This revelation makes her rigid, hyper-vigilant mindset completely understandable and convincing: her harshness stems not from elitist malice, but from her own hard-won experience of how ruthlessly society judges working-class people trying to move up in the world.
